item.title: Anthropic's IPO and stock market risk
item.dc:creator: The Conversation
item.description: • Anthropic’s record US$2 trillion stock market listing highlights the growing risks for all of us • PHP is in the foundation of 70% of websites – here’s what it is and why a flaw in the software is a major hacking threat • People are using AI to make expensive computer programs free. This could change everything • Made in China AI: new tech, same old story? • As AI takes on more tasks, what happens when people have to jump in to clean up after it?
item.content:encoded:
Anthropic’s upcoming entry into the stock market, which it signaled this week by filing paperwork for an initial public offering, is going to make some people a lot of money. For retail investors, though, the high concentration of AI companies in the stock market means that regular people’s investments are exposed to AI-related risks, writes a finance scholar.

Large language models are rapidly reshaping the software industry, as two stories demonstrate this week. The technology was instrumental in identifying a vulnerability in PHP, a language used in millions of websites, and the technology’s ability to reverse engineer existing software packages could upend pricing in the commercial market for apps.

Also this week, a look at whether China’s push into AI will follow the same economic path as other technologies, and what happens to human workers’ skills as they hand off more and more to AI.

Martin LaMonica

Director of Editorial Projects and Newsletters

Webinar

Lead story

Anthropic’s record US$2 trillion stock market listing highlights the growing risks for all of us

Marta Khomyn, Adelaide University

This is the first time a company has come to market warning of ‘catastrophic or existential risks to humanity’.

If consumer and business demand for AI disappoints, tech companies’ bond prices and credit ratings would likely fall together – just as their shares would.

Cybersecurity

PHP is in the foundation of 70% of websites – here’s what it is and why a flaw in the software is a major hacking threat

Doug Jacobson, Iowa State University

A cybersecurity researcher explains how a flaw in widespread software makes millions of websites vulnerable to hackers – and underscores the role of AI in attacking and defending the internet.

Business

People are using AI to make expensive computer programs free. This could change everything

Dana McKay, RMIT University

Some say this will take us back to the cool, weird internet of the 1990s.

Made in China AI: new tech, same old story?

Iordanis Kalaitzoglou, Audencia

History could repeat itself if China turns AI into an abundant, commodity-driven industry. Should we be worried about AI’s new land of plenty?

Work

As AI takes on more tasks, what happens when people have to jump in to clean up after it?

Murugan Anandarajan, Drexel University

Having a human “in the loop” overseeing when an AI makes a decision is important, but what happens to that responsible human over time when the AI gets it right over and over again?

item.title: From psephology to spook-ology
item.dc:creator: The Conversation
item.description: • Israel has voted, but what comes next? Dissecting a messy ballot and coalition-building process • Werewolf mice, ghostly frogs and zombie cockroaches: the animal versions of our Halloween horrors • Medieval ghost stories featured rotten flesh, the walking dead and spoon-stealing spirits • Buried cats, exorcisms and a sunken Colonel Sanders – the strange world of sporting curses • The female scream is now an all-powerful cry in horror films • I’ve been talking to MAGA supporters for years, and here’s why some are sticking with Trump — and others are not • Who mapped Africa? Debunking the myth that Europeans alone plotted the continent • Harry Kane wins Ballon d'Or – a victory for sportsmanship over celebrity
item.content:encoded:
Over the last few days, voters have opted for continuity in Brazil, change in Serbia, and in Israel … well, that is going to take some time to work out.

But today’s newsletter is more about otherworldly matters than global concerns. You see, us editors at The Conversation love Halloween – it is a chance to scour the academic world for research on all things spooky and scary. Take zoologists Alex Dittrich and Kat Hamill’s deep dive into the world of animals that display behaviors common to your favorite horror characters. Here we find cannibal mice that howl at the moon, wasps with the ability to turn prey into zombies and ghostly translucent frogs.

Meanwhile, Vaughan Cruickshank takes a look at how buried cats and spurned goats have contributed to cursed teams and sporting failure. And for those who love a good jump scare, culture scholars Sara Beth Lyons and James Deaville, explore what goes into a good movie scream and how the art of the shriek has evolved over the decades.

Finally, Marcus Librizzi – who collects ghost stories from around the world – explains the deeper meaning to the genre. “These stories can keep alive the memory of a dark past. In my research I have come across tales that preserve memories of injustices that might otherwise have been forgotten,” he writes.

Matt Williams

Senior International Editor

Top story

Gadi Eisenkot or Benjamin Netanyahu – under whose direction will Israel head? Erik Marmor/picture alliance via Getty Images

Israel has voted, but what comes next? Dissecting a messy ballot and coalition-building process

Dov Waxman, University of California, Los Angeles

With no clear majority for the ruling coalition or main opposition bloc, working out who will form the next government could take months.

Spooky stories

Werewolf mice, ghostly frogs and zombie cockroaches: the animal versions of our Halloween horrors

Alex Dittrich, Nottingham Trent University; Kat Hamill, Nottingham Trent University

They have creepy tendencies but these animals are real not fictional.

Medieval ghost stories featured rotten flesh, the walking dead and spoon-stealing spirits

Alex Brown, Durham University

Medieval ghosts shapeshifted, rose from their graves, and begged for help in making amends for their misdeeds.

Buried cats, exorcisms and a sunken Colonel Sanders – the strange world of sporting curses

Vaughan Cruickshank, University of Tasmania

Why would fans of a Japanese baseball team throw a statue of Colonel Sanders into a local canal? Welcome to the world of sporting curses.

The female scream is now an all-powerful cry in horror films

James Deaville, Carleton University; Sara Beth Lyons, Carleton University

As Halloween approaches and horror movies circulate, a look at the legendary ‘scream queens’ and their talent and power.

Non-spooky stories

I’ve been talking to MAGA supporters for years, and here’s why some are sticking with Trump — and others are not

Alex Hinton, Rutgers University - Newark

Despite the headwinds that have cratered support for Donald Trump – high prices, the Iran war, corruption – many of Trump’s MAGA loyalists still back him. A scholar who studies MAGA looks at why.

Who mapped Africa? Debunking the myth that Europeans alone plotted the continent

Thomas J Bassett, University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign

African guides drew lines in the sand to help Europeans understand the terrain. But they rarely got the credit.

Harry Kane wins Ballon d'Or – a victory for sportsmanship over celebrity

Josh Bland, University of Cambridge

Harry Kane represents a hard grafting and unshowy sportsmanship many would like to see as the future of football.

  • King Charles’ visit to the Caribbean evokes specter of British slavery – and local demands for justice

    Brooke N. Newman, Virginia Commonwealth University

    For locals, the king’s Caribbean visit is an occasion to recognize the full story of Britain’s trafficking and enslavement of millions of people across the Atlantic.

  • Indonesia’s El Niño-driven peat fires are choking the region – and releasing centuries of stored carbon

    Gareth Roberts, University of Southampton; Martin Wooster, King's College London

    An intense drought is the match. Decades of deforestation and peat draining provide the fuel.

  • Serbia’s leaderless student movement has won a historic election – but what happens next?

    Eric Gordy, UCL

    With no leader or political experience, Serbia’s student movement now begins talks to form a government.

  • EU’s new Arctic strategy signals shift in its geopolitical mindset

    Emilie Canova, University of Cambridge; Centre national de la recherche scientifique (CNRS)

    The EU has unveiled its first Arctic strategy since Russia’s invasion of Ukraine.

  • Private equity is buying up more methadone clinics – access to the lifesaving drug isn’t getting easier

    Yashaswini Singh, Brown University

    Despite acquiring more than one-third of US methadone clinics, private equity has not significantly expanded methadone availability.

  • How porn became so extreme – and how it’s shaping the sex lives of young people

    Gemma Ware, The Conversation

    Extreme pornography has become readily available on mainstream porn sites. Clare McGlynn explains what this is doing to the sex lives of young people.

item.title: Why voters don't respond to promises of cash
item.dc:creator: The Conversation
item.description: • Offering cash for votes is quite common – but here’s why it doesn’t work • Anthropic’s record US$2 trillion stock market listing highlights the growing risks for all of us • We studied 1,584 data centers – and found the buildings full of machines are tied to modest local job growth • Victorian spiritualism capitalised on the desire to transcend death to create new ways of making money • Halloween meets history in many ghostly tourism attractions. Is this a problem? • Daylight saving was meant to save energy. Do we still need it in the age of LEDs?
item.content:encoded:
President Donald Trump has a long history of offering money to voters – a recent example being his pledge of US$5,000 to every American if Republicans win the November 2026 midterm elections.

His Republican allies in Congress didn’t take action on the proposal, which would cost over $1 trillion. But these cash promises are one thing that Trump has in common with many politicians, past and present, all around the world. Vote buying, in fact, goes back to ancient Rome.

The puzzle is why party leaders still think this is such a good idea, writes Kenneth Greene, a political scientist at the University of Texas-Austin. His research, which looks at vote buying globally but focuses in particular on Mexico, concludes that this practice almost never pays off.

As he explains, whatever cash incentive a party offers has to outweigh a person’s desire to vote their actual preferences – a tall order. It’s also hard for party machines to identify the “right” swing voter, and just as hard to ensure.

There’s also one major downside for democracy, notes Greene. A party may triumph at the polls, but it will never know whether it won because voters believed in its platform or because they expected to get paid.

Helen Fessenden

Senior Economy and Business Editor, The Conversation U.S.

Offering cash for votes is quite common – but here’s why it doesn’t work

Kenneth Greene, The University of Texas at Austin

Money or other material benefits are often not enough to override a voter’s preferences and partisanship.

Essential briefings

Anthropic’s record US$2 trillion stock market listing highlights the growing risks for all of us

Marta Khomyn, Adelaide University

This is the first time a company has come to market warning of ‘catastrophic or existential risks to humanity’.

We studied 1,584 data centers – and found the buildings full of machines are tied to modest local job growth

Simon Buechler, Miami University; Lyndsey Rolheiser, York University, Canada

This employment boost took three to five years to show up, two researchers found after studying more than two decades of data.

Victorian spiritualism capitalised on the desire to transcend death to create new ways of making money

James Cronin, Lancaster University; Sophie James, Lancaster University

The very technologies that transformed Victorian commerce and entertainment also helped make ghosts visible, reproducible and profitable.

Halloween meets history in many ghostly tourism attractions. Is this a problem?

Ann-Kathrin McLean, Royal Roads University; Juan Claudio Benavides del Carpio, Royal Roads University

All attractions situated along a ‘dark tourism spectrum’ must carefully navigate questions about respectful engagement and exploitation.

Quote of the week

The original justification for daylight saving time as an energy-saving measure is increasingly uncertain. Broadly, research suggests reductions in lighting demand are most likely to be balanced by increased heating and cooling demand. Any energy savings are likely to be relatively small and depend on factors beyond lighting efficiency.

—

Amin Al-Habaibeh, Professor of Intelligent Engineering Systems, Nottingham Trent University

Daylight saving was meant to save energy. Do we still need it in the age of LEDs?

Technology

  • Shares in this data centre company are down 40% as investors lose faith in the AI story

    Andrew Cullen, The University of Melbourne

    While AI hype is strong, the business models are coming under increasing scrutiny.

  • How should AI be regulated? Follow the harm

    Sylvia Lu, American University

    Instead of trying to restrict AI technologies, regulations could focus on the harm the technology causes people and companies.

  • Data centers are inspiring bipartisanship – for now

    Barbara A. Trish, Grinnell College

    A political scientist who studies AI in campaigns explains why data centers have put Bernie Sanders and Steve Bannon on the same side ahead of the midterms.

  • AI chatbots can be a valuable health resource for older adults – if they embrace ‘informed skepticism’

    Robin Brewer, University of Michigan

    AI can help you navigate health information, but evaluating the credibility and quality of responses is key.

Personal finance

  • The psychology that can lead investors to make bad financial decisions

    Donald Amuah, University of South Wales

    Recent research suggests even people training for careers in finance can fall prey to overconfidence, loss aversion and other psychological biases.

Economy

  • How El Niño could push up your mortgage and grocery bills

    Narmin Nahidi, University of Exeter

    A Pacific climate event has far reaching effects.

  • Zimbabwe wants digital payments to build trust in its newest currency. Why technology alone won’t be enough to save the ZiG

    Jonathan Munemo, Salisbury University

    Zimbabwe’s goal should be to promote wider adoption of the local currency, not to use technology to force it.

item.title: Voters make their mark
item.dc:creator: The Conversation
item.description: • Lula wins a ‘miracle’ election in Brazil. Now comes the hard part: putting the country back on the right track • ‘We changed the system’: how Serbian students ended Alexander Vučić’s 12 years in power • Why ultra-Orthodox parties hold so much sway in Israeli politics • Palestinian citizens face a painful choice in Israel’s election: To vote or not
item.content:encoded:
A big week for elections got off to a bang on Sunday when Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva pulled off a dramatic comeback to win Brazil’s presidential poll, beating rightwing challenger Flávio Bolsonaro by a whisker. Lula gained 51.79 per cent of votes against 48.21 per cent for the son of jailed ex-president Jair Bolsonaro, in a two-way run-off in Latin America’s largest democracy.

As Guilherme Casarões points out, now comes the hard part for the 80-year-old Lula as he starts his fourth term in office.

On Monday it was Serbia’s turn. A grassroots Student List won up to 140 of the Serbian parliament’s 250 seats, marking a dramatic defeat for strongman and nationalist president Aleksandar Vučić. Gavin Brent Sullivan and Tereza Capelos explain the Student List’s remarkable story.

And today Israel goes to the polls in an election that will have consequences beyond the country’s borders. Hannah Ridge unpacks why ultra-Orthodox parties hold so much sway while Tamir Sorek explains the painful choice faced by Palestinian citizens - whether to vote, or whether to boycott the poll.

Caroline Southey

Founding Editor, Africa

Lula wins a ‘miracle’ election in Brazil. Now comes the hard part: putting the country back on the right track

Guilherme Casarões, Florida International University

The real antidote to polarisation will not come from a single election or a single leader.

‘We changed the system’: how Serbian students ended Alexander Vučić’s 12 years in power

Gavin Brent Sullivan, International Psychoanalytic University Berlin; Tereza Capelos, University of Southampton

A record number of voters turned out to end Alexander Vučić’s longstanding dominance of Serbian politics.

Why ultra-Orthodox parties hold so much sway in Israeli politics

Hannah Ridge, Chapman University; Institute for Humane Studies

Ultra-Orthodox Jews, often called Haredim, make up a small but growing percentage of Israel’s population. Still, their political parties wield significant influence.

Palestinian citizens face a painful choice in Israel’s election: To vote or not

Tamir Sorek, Penn State

More than a third of Israel’s Palestinian citizens are expected to sit out the election.

  • UN peacekeepers prepare to exit Lebanon after 70 years – leaving behind a worrying security vacuum

    Mireille Rebeiz, Dickinson College; University of Otago

    In August, the UN Security Council voted to end the decades-long peacekeeping mission in Lebanon. Blue helmets will leave by the end of the year.

  • PHP is in the foundation of 70% of websites – here’s what it is and why a flaw in the software is a major hacking threat

    Doug Jacobson, Iowa State University

    A cybersecurity researcher explains how a flaw in widespread software makes millions of websites vulnerable to hackers – and underscores the role of AI in attacking and defending the internet.

  • Stanford prison experiment: why do controversial psychology studies still have such a hold on us?

    David Kaposi, The Open University

    A new Netflix series has revived interest in the Stanford prison experiment. Zimbardo and Milgram’s flawed studies still leave a question unanswered.

  • Why do people still get polio in some countries and not in others?

    Katrine L. Wallace, University of Illinois Chicago

    Polio can survive only where it finds kids who aren’t protected by a vaccine.

item.title: Brazil's pivotal presidential runoff
item.dc:creator: The Conversation
item.description: • Brazil’s election puts at risk country’s role as a bulwark against Trump interventionism in the Americas • How Lula turned 4 lessons from the elections in Colombia into a comeback campaign in Brazil • Faith, rhetoric and the ballot box: How religion has shaped Brazil’s current presidential election • Youth protests across Europe: the overlapping crises facing Gen Z • From elite spies to ‘gig-economy’ operatives: the changing face of Russian sabotage • Palestinian citizens face a painful choice in Israel’s election: To vote or not
item.content:encoded:
Brazilians head back to the polls on Sunday to vote in a second round of the country’s presidential election. The choice is between incumbent President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva and his far-right opponent Flávio Bolsonaro, son of the jailed former president, Jair Bolsonaro

The outcome of this tight race – which may be decided by a few hundred thousand votes in a electorate of more than 158.7 million – will have repercussions that go far beyond the country’s borders.

Dawisson Belém Lopes, a professor of international and comparative politics at the Federal University of Minas Gerais, argues that a possible win by Bolsonaro puts at risk Brazil’s role as a bulwark against Trump interventionism in the Americas, alongside Mexico and Canada. Since the start of the U.S. president’s second term in January 2025, country after country in the region has succumbed to the U.S. government’s meddling and interference, in a phenomenon known international relations as “peripheral realism.”

Meanwhile, Florida International University’s Guilherme Casarões and Carlos Ricaurte see hope for a Lula comeback after his first round defeat, having learned the lessons from another recent tight presidential race victory by a far-right candidate in South America: Abelardo de la Espriella in Colombia. But to win, Lula will need to overcome attempts to influence the results by a political venture capital firm founded by U.S. Vice President J.D. Vance, as well as the rise of Evangelical Christians as a political force for the conservative movement in the country.

Cesar Baima

Editor

Top story

Peripheral realism: Judging by the crowds at oposition candidate Flávio Bolsonaro’s rallies, the idea of aligning Brazil with U.S. interventionist interests is well accepted by his voters, but if incumbent President Lula is reelected, sovereign resistance is likely to continue. AP Photo/Andre Penner

Brazil’s election puts at risk country’s role as a bulwark against Trump interventionism in the Americas

Dawisson Belém Lopes, Universidade Federal de Minas Gerais (UFMG)

A victory for Flávio Bolsonaro could keep Brazil trapped in a model of extractivism that has been part of the country’s history since the arrival of the Portuguese settlers in the 16th century.

How Lula turned 4 lessons from the elections in Colombia into a comeback campaign in Brazil

Guilherme Casarões, Florida International University; Carlos Ricaurte, Florida International University

Iván Cepeda’s defeat in Colombia served as a wake-up call for the left in Brazil. The campaign shifted its focus from rhetoric about sovereignty to issues that directly affect people’s daily lives, pushing foreign policy into the background

Faith, rhetoric and the ballot box: How religion has shaped Brazil’s current presidential election

Manuela Lowenthal, Universidade Federal de São Paulo (UNIFESP)

In Brazil, religion is the dominant cultural grammar. More than a simple expression of individual faith, religion functions in politics as a sociolinguistic marker of order and authority.

Youth protests across Europe: the overlapping crises facing Gen Z

Alina Cosma, Trinity College Dublin

Young people appear to be facing increasing demands while some of the social resources that help them cope are weakening.

From elite spies to ‘gig-economy’ operatives: the changing face of Russian sabotage

Elena Grossfeld, King's College London; Swedish Defence University

Across domains, Russia has turned unpredictability and disruption into its strategic weapon of choice.

Palestinian citizens face a painful choice in Israel’s election: To vote or not

Tamir Sorek, Penn State

More than a third of Israel’s Palestinian citizens are expected to sit out the election.

  • America’s death penalty: why executions are rising again

    Grace Jennings-Edquist, The Conversation; Justin Bergman, The Conversation

    Death penalty expert Carolyn Strange tracks the modern history of executions in the United States on The Conversation Weekly podcast.

  • A critical flaw affecting 70% of all websites has the cybersecurity world panicked

    Andrew Cullen, The University of Melbourne

    Millions of websites and online tools have relied on the PHP language for decades – but newly disclosed bugs could let hackers easily take them over.

  • Napoleon can be partly blamed for Gen Z’s weightlifting obsession – here’s why

    Claire Warden, Loughborough University; Conor Heffernan, Ulster University

    Just as fitness trends have changed, so too have the reasons behind why people exercise.

  • How K-dramas use Africa as a backdrop to boost South Korea’s image

    Osarugue Otebele, University of Toronto

    Africa constantly appears as a ‘country’ full of savage danger or childish rebellion, in need of a saviour.

  • Hokusai’s Great Wave is one of 46 prints of Mount Fuji – seeing them together changes everything

    Dominik Havsteen-Franklin, Brunel University of London

    The prints create a story that expands our understanding of the now famous Great Wave.

  • Unlocking the secrets of the ‘Dragon Man’ skull – and what it reveals about human evolution

    Chris Stringer, UCL; Natural History Museum

    Most of what we knew about early modern humans has been turned upside down in the past two decades – and many more questions remain.

item.title: AI's roots in cognitive science explain how it works
item.dc:creator: The Conversation
item.description: • AI behaves more like a brain than a database – cognitive science’s role in its origin story helps explain why • Who’s paying whom? The circular money machine behind the AI boom (or bubble) • Why calling for a ‘kill switch’ is the wrong way to think about reining in AI • Using an AI chatbot to practice new languages can be helpful, but it doesn’t replace speaking with an actual person • Can AI screen for heart disease using photos of your tongue and face?
item.content:encoded:
Large language models bring a fundamental change to how people interact with computers: Instead of a system based on rules to, for example, find a piece of information in a database, artificial intelligence systems act on examples and probability, write two cognitive scientists, who argue that understanding the technology’s roots provides a helpful mental model for using AI. Also this week, a look at the so-called circular deals fueling AI spending, how chatbots can accelerate language learning, an experiment to screen for heart disease based on photos, and, amid growing alarm over AI systems acting outside human control, why the kill switch metaphor falls short in setting policy.

Lead story

AI behaves more like a brain than a database – cognitive science’s role in its origin story helps explain why

Michael Hout, New Mexico State University; Arryn Robbins, University of Richmond

Modern AI owes its existence to both cognitive and computer science. What you envision as its origin story can influence how you understand what large language models can do.

Thinking of AI as like a primitive brain helps explain additional puzzling behaviors, such as getting different answers to the same question. Ask your young child what they want for dinner twice and you may get different requests.

Business

Who’s paying whom? The circular money machine behind the AI boom (or bubble)

Ruipeng Liu, Deakin University; Sagarika Mishra, Deakin University

What’s not clear is how much of this AI boom is being driven by real, end-user demand — and how much might be a bubble.

Policy

Why calling for a ‘kill switch’ is the wrong way to think about reining in AI

Trent Wintermeier, The University of Texas at Austin

A kill switch to shut down dangerous AI systems is a seductive concept, but the metaphor hides how the models work – and how they get out of control in the first place.

Education

Using an AI chatbot to practice new languages can be helpful, but it doesn’t replace speaking with an actual person

Antonio Perez-Nunez, College of Charleston

People might feel more comfortable making mistakes if they’re interacting with AI chatbots. But they will miss the nuances that come from conversing with real people.

Science

Can AI screen for heart disease using photos of your tongue and face?

David C. Gaze, University of Westminster

Photos of the face and tongue helped an AI identify heart disease with 98% accuracy, but screening the general public is a much harder task.

item.title: How Biden's climate bill helped some Republicans
item.dc:creator: The Conversation
item.description: • Federal spending on climate change before 2024 election boosted incumbents of both parties • US inequality is getting worse in ways you might not expect • Americans want electric cars – they just can’t find them • A scuff on your bag, a dent in your mug – and suddenly it feels like time for a new one • Remote work made these colleagues more open with each other, not less • How governments worldwide are shaping what AI can say about politics
item.content:encoded:
“Pork barrel” spending – sending public money to projects to shore up political support – is a time-honored American tradition of Republicans and Democrats alike.

But sometimes it has surprising results, as political scientist Kayla Morton of the University of Delaware explains.

Her case in point is the 2022 Inflation Reduction Act, President Joe Biden’s signature climate bill that channeled US$370 billion to clean energy projects. Not a single Republican voted for it, but about 80% of those funds went to Republican districts. The hope among Democrats was that it would create jobs and push more Republican voters to support a green agenda while giving Democratic politicians a major policy win to tout.

In a way, this strategy worked – but not always to the Democrats’ benefit. Morton found that both Democratic and Republican incumbents did better in the 2024 elections if their district got Inflation Reduction Act funds, everything else being equal. So while Democrats could claim that the legislation was a political win, it didn’t give them an edge over Republicans.

“Voters may reward investments even when the policies that created them remain politically contentious,” she concludes. “Economic investments in fighting climate change can generate local political benefits across party lines.”

Helen Fessenden

Senior Economy and Business Editor, The Conversation U.S.

Federal spending on climate change before 2024 election boosted incumbents of both parties

Kayla Morton, University of Delaware

Incumbents can still reap electoral rewards when federal money reaches their districts, even if they opposed the bill that provided it.

Essential briefings

US inequality is getting worse in ways you might not expect

Markus Schneider, University of Denver

From tax policy to gas prices and tariffs, a mix of new factors is making inequality in the US more extreme.

Americans want electric cars – they just can’t find them

John Paul Helveston, George Washington University

Sales reveal how many cars people actually bought, but not how many they actually wanted. Prices, on the other hand, show how demand is changing.

A scuff on your bag, a dent in your mug – and suddenly it feels like time for a new one

Rebecca Walker Reczek, The Ohio State University; Aprajita Gautam, Texas A&M University; Rajagopal Raghunathan, The University of Texas at Austin

While perfectionists hold themselves to high or even impossible standards, people who want perfect stuff hold what they buy and own to lofty standards.

Remote work made these colleagues more open with each other, not less

Vanessa M. Conzon, Boston College

Remote work does not necessarily mean that social connections break down. Instead, it can provide the spark for stronger and better relationships between co-workers.

Quote of the week

When you ask your chatbot about the elections, treat the answer as a starting point. Keep in mind that governments, both foreign and domestic, may try to influence the answer. AI responses should not replace your critical thinking at the ballot box.

—

Jordi Calvet-Bademunt, Research Fellow and Visiting Scholar of Political Science, Vanderbilt University

How governments worldwide are shaping what AI can say about politics

Economy

  • Is the world pricing the risk of a US diesel export ban?

    Michel Robe, University of Richmond

    If the US imposed a ban on its diesel exports, as some lawmakers are calling for, it would roil the global market.

  • How buying weapons can harm a country’s economy

    Tomasz Piotr Wisniewski, The Open University; Ayman Omar, University of Leicester; Cristiana Bernardi, The Open University

    Investors are wary of potential conflict.

  • When tax officials visit: why softer tax outreach can build trust in some places and erode it in others

    Christopher Hoy, The University of Melbourne; Revocatus Paul, University of Cape Town

    Building the tax base in low-capacity settings is about making the state more visible and more credible.

Inequality

  • Childhood adversity linked to billions in health and economic costs – new research

    Kat Ford, Bangor University; Liverpool John Moores University; Karen Hughes, Bangor University

    The health effects of childhood adversity carry a huge economic burden, according to new research across Wales and England.

Work

  • Looking for work as a disabled person? Recognize your strengths and find an accessible workplace

    Erika Katzman, Western University

    Disabled job seekers bring valuable skills to work. Here’s how to recognize those strengths, assess employers and advocate for accessible workplaces.

Consumers

  • New AI shopping agents promise better bargains. But who pays the price?

    Lynnaire Sheridan, University of Otago

    As AI agents begin shopping on our behalf, there’s a real risk cheaper products could put more pressure on vulnerable workers in global supply chains.

Technology

  • Why calling for a ‘kill switch’ is the wrong way to think about reining in AI

    Trent Wintermeier, The University of Texas at Austin

    A kill switch to shut down dangerous AI systems is a seductive concept, but the metaphor hides how the models work – and how they get out of control in the first place.

  • Can social media bans protect young people’s mental health? Early research suggests that bans aren’t the answer

    Ari Lightman, Carnegie Mellon University

    Kids have found ways around most of the safeguards meant to keep them off social media platforms.

item.title: Violent protests bolster France's political extremes
item.dc:creator: The Conversation
item.description: • As French protests escalate into riots, they may prove a gift for Marine Le Pen’s right-wing party • Millions of children aren’t getting vaccinated: how mapping tools can help find them
item.content:encoded:
After weeks of mostly peaceful protests in France over the rising cost of living and underfunded public services, things took a violent turn on Saturday. Police were unable to contain rioting, looting and the widespread destruction of public facilities and businesses. On Monday, curfews were put in place in a number of cities, including Paris.

As Peter McPhee writes, the immediate issue is whether Emmanuel Macron’s beleaguered government can defuse the tensions within a deeply angry society. With six months to go to the presidential election, the protests and violent clashes have bolstered France’s political extremes while undermining the centre. For far-right leader Marine Le Pen, the sense of a government losing control is a gift.

Vaccination is one of the most important and effective public health interventions in history. It’s estimated that immunisation saves up to 5 million lives every year. item.content:encoded:
Japan is leading a group of agencies on a slightly different route to Mars. A robotic mission due to launch Monday will target Phobos, one of the red planet’s two small moons. Martian Moons Exploration (MMX) aims to bring samples of rock and soil back to Earth in 2031, potentially solving the mystery of how Mars acquired its moons.

Daniel Brown, lecturer in astronomy at Nottingham Trent University, England, explains the engineering involved – from deploying a tiny rover to collecting material in Phobos’s remarkably weak gravity. The mission is also a reminder of how much we can learn by bringing extraterrestrial material back to Earth for lab analysis. With NASA’s much more ambitious Mars Sample Return programme effectively cancelled, MMX could offer scientists an unexpected consolation prize: a glimpse into the geological history of Mars without ever touching down on the planet.

Elsewhere this week, we have been keeping track on Starlink’s slowdown in Ukraine and talking about separatism in Canada’s Alberta.

item.title: Will a consolidated American media landscape leave voters less informed?
item.dc:creator: The Conversation
item.description: • Why the Paramount-Warner merger is a problem for democracy • Turmoil within Dolly Parton’s estate underscores the precariousness of family businesses after founders die • Economics Nobel: how this year’s winners helped to smooth the cycle of economic peaks and troughs • Who’s paying whom? The circular money machine behind the AI boom (or bubble) • Why your boss matters more than remote or hybrid work when it comes to burnout and job satisfaction • Advertising like Sydney Sweeney’s Novig campaign teach women to see themselves as objects
item.content:encoded:
Are free markets good for a free press?

The United States has long allowed a largely private, commercial broadcasting system to dominate, while other countries, including the U.K., also offered a public alternative. One result has been intense concentration of market players, the most recent example being the behemoth US$110 billion deal between Paramount and Warner Bros. Discovery.

The new company, Skydance Corporation, now owns CNN and CBS News, Warner Bros. and Paramount Pictures, HBO and Paramount+, and a slew of other assets.

The economies of scale mean that these giants can compete better against platforms such as Netflix and YouTube. But as Seth Ashley of Colorado State University writes, the same pressures driving consolidation can also “undermine the independent reporting and diversity of voices that democracy depends on.”

While mergers may make economic sense, they don’t necessarily make citizens better informed. One example is what happened after the Sinclair Broadcast Group acquired local television stations under a 2017 deal. Less political competition and lower voter participation in elections followed the drop-off in local media coverage.

“Democracy assumes that citizens will have enough information to make choices and hold powerful institutions accountable,” writes Ashley, a journalism scholar. “But markets provide no guarantee that anyone will produce it.”

item.title: Severe COVID and children's genes
item.dc:creator: The Conversation
item.description: • Why do some children become seriously ill with COVID? The answer may lie in their genes • How a botched execution and proposed livestream of a firing squad fit in to the US’ death penalty history
item.content:encoded:
It’s three years since the end of the COVID pandemic, yet researchers continue to grapple with questions about the virus. One relates to the severity of infections in children. While most children who become infected with COVID only experience mild symptoms, others develop a severe infection that can, in some instances, lead to hospitalisation.

Until now, it hasn’t been clear what factors may be behind this. But new research from experts at the University of Southampton and the University of Cape Town suggests that the answer may lie in their genes.

Two recent cases in the US have triggered heated debates about the death penalty. The first was the botched execution of convicted murderer Christa Pike in Tennessee. The second was the announcement by Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth that the execution of US Army major Nidal Hasan, sentenced to death for 13 murders, would be live-streamed. Hasan is due to be executed by firing squad on December 3rd.

Death penalty expert Carolyn Strange places these cases in America’s long and complex history with the death penalty and the politics that surround it.

Heather Kroeker

Commissioning Editor, Health + Medicine

item.title: Is AI becoming a new religion?
item.dc:creator: The Conversation
item.description: • Why AI resembles a charismatic religious leader • Why a decade of AI safety promises keep failing to bite • Trump wants an AI Force like Space Force, but that could make AI’s risks harder to manage • Why most health apps are biased even before their first lines of code are written • We’ve tracked $80M of spending on almost 170 AI-generated political ads this year – it’s weird
item.content:encoded:
What happens when a person moves from asking a chatbot for emotional support and advice to spiritual guidance? AI is already transforming the practice of religion in many ways, but a scholar of religion delves into whether AI represents a new kind of religious movement. Also this week, a couple of articles examine the daunting challenges regulating AI technology at an international level, another piece examines the bias inherent in AI-infused health monitoring apps, and a look at the varied – and sometimes odd – ways AI is shaking up political campaigns in the U.S.

Lead Story

Why AI resembles a charismatic religious leader

Morgan Shipley, Michigan State University

AI can function as a charismatic figure without standing on a stage, establishing a church or gathering disciples, writes a scholar of religion.

At this point, AI clearly offers something more significant than access to information. By helping people interpret their lives, AI is entering territory historically occupied by therapists, spiritual advisers and religious communities.
